newsitem.title: USA: Calif measure not seen hurting current L.A. budget.
newsitem.headline: Calif measure not seen hurting current L.A. budget.

text.p: A controversial California tax measure approved by voters earlier this month should not hurt Los Angeles County's 1996-1997 budget, according to county report released on Monday.

"All existing assessments, fees and charges may be collected through June 30, 1997," county Chief Administrative Officer David Janssen said in a report to county supervisors. Proposition 218, approved by voters on November 5, strengthens existing law to require local taxes be submitted to voters for approval. It also allows property owners to approve assessments and strictly limits use of fees and charges.

Janssen said the impact on the county's 1997-1998 budget and on subsequent fiscal years would vary depending on the final judicial or legislative interpretation of Proposition 218 and voter response to future tax measures.
He said county amusement park and landfill tipping taxes, as well as increases to the business license and transient occupancy taxes must now be submitted to voters.
The county also has assessments for fire departments, libraries, flood control, street lighting, landscape maintenance and regional parks.
"We believe that all but the assessments for fire and libraries are exempted by specific provision of Proposition 218 from its requirements," Janssen said.
Proposition 218 has drawn fire from local government officials throughout California.

The Los Angeles City Council recently decided to sue over the California measure. Los Angeles could be the first local government to go to court over the proposition, but was not expected to be the last to sue.
Moody's Investors Service Inc has warned that the credit ratings of some local governments in the state could be undermined by the tax measure.
